questions.stem: A 28-year-old researcher studies the percentage of filtered sodium reabsorbed at each segment of the nephron, summarized in the diagram below. At which of the following segments is the largest fraction of filtered sodium reabsorbed?
questions.diagram:
Sodium reabsorption along the nephron
PCT (~65%) → Loop of Henle (~25%) → DCT (~5%) → CD principal cells (~3%)
Glomerular filtrate is iso-osmotic with plasma; reabsorption is largely isosmotic in PCT and dilutes fluid in TAL.
choices: Distal convoluted tubule (DCT)
Proximal convoluted tubule (PCT)
Cortical and medullary collecting duct
Thick ascending limb of Henle (TAL)
Thin descending limb of Henle
explanations: Incorrect. The DCT reabsorbs only ~5% of filtered Na+, but is critical for fine-tuning and is the site of action of thiazide diuretics.

Correct. The PCT reabsorbs the largest fraction of filtered Na+ — approximately 65% — driven by basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase, with apical NHE3 and Na+-coupled cotransporters (glucose, amino acids, phosphate). PCT reabsorption is largely isosmotic with the filtrate. Quantitative reabsorption thereafter is ~25% in TAL, ~5% in DCT, ~3% in collecting duct principal cells.
Incorrect. The collecting duct reabsorbs only ~3% of filtered Na+, but its activity is regulated by aldosterone and is the principal site of fine adjustment.
Incorrect. The TAL reabsorbs ~25% via NKCC2 and is the major diluting segment, but it is not the largest reabsorptive segment.
Incorrect. The thin descending limb is permeable to water but does not reabsorb Na+ actively.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old physiologist studies glucose reabsorption in the proximal convoluted tubule. Which of the following best describes the relative contributions of SGLT2 (sodium-glucose cotransporter 2) versus SGLT1 to total glucose reabsorption in the PCT?
choices: SGLT2 reabsorbs ~10%, SGLT1 reabsorbs ~90%
SGLT2 reabsorbs ~30%, SGLT1 reabsorbs ~70%
SGLT2 and SGLT1 each reabsorb ~50%
SGLT2 reabsorbs ~90%, SGLT1 reabsorbs ~10%
SGLT2 reabsorbs ~100%, SGLT1 plays no role
explanations: Incorrect. The contributions of SGLT2 and SGLT1 are reversed: SGLT2 dominates, not SGLT1.
Incorrect. SGLT2 is the dominant transporter (~90%); SGLT1 plays a smaller role.
Incorrect. The two transporters do not contribute equally.

Correct. SGLT2, located in the apical membrane of the early proximal convoluted tubule (S1/S2 segments), reabsorbs ~90% of filtered glucose. SGLT1, in the late PCT (S3 segment), captures most of the remaining ~10%. Pharmacologic inhibition of SGLT2 (e.g., empagliflozin) therefore produces clinically significant glucosuria. Note that under physiologic plasma glucose, both transporters together fully reabsorb glucose; glucosuria appears only when filtered load exceeds Tm-glucose.
Incorrect. SGLT1 also contributes (~10%) and is responsible for limited residual reabsorption in late PCT.

questions.stem: A 22-year-old woman with diabetic ketoacidosis has a plasma glucose of 580 mg/dL and significant glycosuria. Glucose reabsorption in the proximal tubule is performed predominantly by which of the following mechanisms?
choices: GLUT2 facilitated diffusion alone in the apical membrane
Insulin-dependent GLUT4 transporters
Direct ATP-dependent glucose pump in the apical membrane
Facilitated diffusion via SGLT proteins independent of sodium
Sodium-glucose cotransport via SGLT2/SGLT1 powered by basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase
explanations: Incorrect. GLUT2 is the BASOLATERAL exit transporter for glucose; it is not the apical entry mechanism.
Incorrect. GLUT4 is the insulin-dependent muscle and adipose transporter and does not function in the renal tubule.
Incorrect. There is no direct ATP-driven glucose pump in the apical membrane; renal glucose reabsorption is secondary active.
Incorrect. SGLT2 and SGLT1 are sodium-DEPENDENT cotransporters; sodium movement provides the driving force.

Correct. Apical SGLT2 (S1/S2) and SGLT1 (S3) cotransport Na+ and glucose into the cell, exploiting the sodium electrochemical gradient established by basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase (secondary active transport). Glucose then exits the basolateral membrane down its concentration gradient via GLUT2 (and GLUT1 in the late PCT). When filtered load exceeds the saturation capacity (Tm-glucose ~375 mg/min), glycosuria appears.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old researcher studies the proximal convoluted tubule. The apical Na+/H+ exchanger (NHE3) couples cellular extrusion of H+ with luminal reabsorption of Na+. Which of the following provides the immediate energy that drives NHE3 activity?
choices: Direct hydrolysis of ATP at NHE3 itself
The Na+ gradient established by basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase
Intracellular CO2 hydration to bicarbonate
An apical proton-ATPase
Cotransport with glucose via SGLT2
explanations: Incorrect. NHE3 is not an ATPase; it does not directly hydrolyze ATP.

Correct. NHE3 is a SECONDARY active transporter. The basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase consumes ATP to maintain a low intracellular Na+, creating a steep Na+ gradient from lumen into cell. NHE3 exploits this gradient: Na+ moves down its gradient INTO the cell, while H+ is exchanged OUT into the lumen. The same principle underlies the energy supply for SGLT, NaPi-IIa, NCC, and other Na+-coupled transporters along the nephron.
Incorrect. CO2 hydration (catalyzed by carbonic anhydrase) provides H+ for secretion but does not drive NHE3 directly.
Incorrect. The apical H+-ATPase is principally a feature of α-intercalated cells in the collecting duct; in the PCT, NHE3 is the main H+ secretion mechanism.
Incorrect. NHE3 is not coupled to glucose transport.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman with metabolic acidosis is being studied. The proximal convoluted tubule reclaims approximately 80% of filtered bicarbonate. Which of the following enzymes is critical for this reclamation process?
choices: Carbonic anhydrase II (cytosolic) and IV (apical brush border)
Glutamine synthetase
Lactate dehydrogenase
Pyruvate kinase
Glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase
explanations: Correct. Bicarbonate reclamation in the PCT works as follows: filtered HCO3− in the lumen combines with H+ secreted by NHE3 to form H2CO3, which is rapidly dehydrated by apical brush-border carbonic anhydrase IV to CO2 + H2O. CO2 diffuses into the cell, where cytosolic carbonic anhydrase II hydrates it back to HCO3− + H+; HCO3− exits the basolateral membrane via the Na+-HCO3− cotransporter (NBCe1), returning to blood. Inhibition of carbonic anhydrase (acetazolamide) impairs this process and produces a self-limited bicarbonate diuresis with metabolic acidosis.
Incorrect. Glutamine synthetase generates glutamine in the liver; the kidney USES glutamine for ammoniagenesis, but this is not the bicarbonate-reclamation step.
Incorrect. Lactate dehydrogenase is involved in lactate metabolism, not HCO3− handling.
Incorrect. Pyruvate kinase is a glycolytic enzyme.
Incorrect. G6PD is the rate-limiting enzyme of the pentose phosphate pathway; it is unrelated to bicarbonate reclamation.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with glaucoma is treated with acetazolamide. The same drug is also used for high-altitude sickness and as a urinary alkalinizer for certain poisonings. Which of the following best describes the renal mechanism of acetazolamide?
choices: Inhibition of NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb
Inhibition of NCC in the distal convoluted tubule
Inhibition of carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
Antagonism of the mineralocorticoid receptor
Inhibition of ENaC in collecting duct principal cells
explanations: Incorrect. NKCC2 inhibition is the mechanism of loop diuretics (furosemide, bumetanide, ethacrynic acid).
Incorrect. NCC inhibition is the mechanism of thiazide diuretics.

Correct. Acetazolamide inhibits carbonic anhydrase (both apical CA-IV and cytosolic CA-II) in the proximal tubule, blocking the reclamation of filtered bicarbonate. This produces a bicarbonate diuresis with alkalinized urine and a non-anion-gap (hyperchloremic) metabolic acidosis. The diuresis is self-limited because as serum HCO3− falls, the filtered load also falls. Acetazolamide is used in glaucoma (reduces aqueous humor formation), altitude sickness (alkalinization of CSF stimulates ventilation), and urinary alkalinization for weak-acid poisonings.
Incorrect. MR antagonism is the mechanism of spironolactone/eplerenone.
Incorrect. ENaC inhibition is the mechanism of amiloride and triamterene.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old man with primary hyperparathyroidism has elevated parathyroid hormone, hypercalcemia, and hypophosphatemia. Phosphate is reabsorbed in the proximal tubule by the apical NaPi-IIa cotransporter. Which of the following best explains how PTH lowers serum phosphate?
choices: PTH directly increases renal blood flow, raising filtered load of phosphate
PTH activates carbonic anhydrase, secondarily affecting phosphate handling
PTH stimulates intestinal phosphate absorption
PTH inhibits the apical NaPi-IIa cotransporter in the PCT
PTH increases proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption directly
explanations: Incorrect. PTH does not principally raise RBF; the phosphaturia is caused by direct effects on the PCT phosphate transporter.
Incorrect. Carbonic anhydrase activity is not the principal target of PTH.
Incorrect. PTH actually increases intestinal Ca2+ and phosphate absorption indirectly via 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D, but this would tend to raise (not lower) serum phosphate.

Correct. PTH binds its receptor (PTHR1) on the basolateral membrane of PCT cells, activating PKA and PKC pathways that promote endocytosis and degradation of apical NaPi-IIa cotransporters. Reduced cotransporter density lowers proximal phosphate reabsorption, producing phosphaturia and hypophosphatemia. Importantly, PTH also raises serum calcium (by stimulating distal tubular Ca2+ reabsorption via TRPV5/calbindin in the DCT and bone resorption), the converse effect on Ca2+.
Incorrect. PTH DECREASES proximal phosphate reabsorption — the opposite of this option.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man develops oliguric acute kidney injury after a course of gentamicin for endocarditis. Renal biopsy shows necrosis predominantly in the proximal convoluted tubule. Which of the following best explains the susceptibility of the PCT to drug-induced and ischemic injury?
choices: The PCT has high metabolic workload and avidly takes up filtered drugs
The PCT operates at the lowest tissue oxygen tension in the kidney
The PCT receives less blood flow than any other nephron segment
The PCT lacks tight junctions, allowing toxins to bypass the cell entirely
PCT cells lack mitochondria
explanations: Correct. The PCT performs the bulk of the nephron's active transport — reabsorbing ~65% of filtered Na+, nearly all glucose and amino acids, ~80% of HCO3−, and large amounts of phosphate, calcium, and urate. This high metabolic workload is supported by abundant mitochondria, making PCT cells vulnerable to ischemia. In addition, megalin–cubilin–mediated endocytosis at the brush border avidly takes up filtered low-molecular-weight molecules — including aminoglycosides, contrast agents, cisplatin, and heavy metals — concentrating them intracellularly. Together these features make the PCT the most common site of drug-induced and ischemic acute tubular necrosis (alongside the medullary thick ascending limb).
Incorrect. The OUTER MEDULLA (and TAL) operates at the lowest PO2; the PCT in the cortex has higher tissue oxygenation.
Incorrect. The cortex (where PCT resides) receives the majority of renal blood flow.
Incorrect. The PCT has tight junctions (albeit 'leaky' ones rich in claudin-2) and continuous epithelium.
Incorrect. PCT cells are mitochondria-RICH because of the high metabolic demand.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher studies the thin descending limb of Henle. AQP1 is expressed apically and basolaterally; there is no significant active transport. As tubular fluid descends through the medullary interstitium, which is progressively more concentrated, water is removed from the tubular fluid. Which of the following best explains the direction and mechanism of water movement in this segment?
choices: Active transport by Na+/K+-ATPase pumping water against its gradient
ADH-stimulated insertion of AQP2 in the apical membrane
Passive osmotic equilibration through constitutive AQP1 channels
Active Cl− pumping that secondarily removes water
K+ recycling through ROMK that drives water reabsorption
explanations: Incorrect. Water cannot be moved by Na+/K+-ATPase against its osmotic gradient; water movement is always passive, following osmolar gradients.
Incorrect. AQP2 is the ADH-regulated water channel of the COLLECTING DUCT principal cell, not of the thin descending limb.

Correct. The thin descending limb of Henle constitutively expresses AQP1 in both apical and basolateral membranes. As tubular fluid descends through the medulla — where the interstitial osmolality progressively rises (due to NaCl and urea deposited by the loops of Henle and ADH-driven urea recycling) — water moves passively out of the tubular fluid down its osmotic gradient. By the bottom of the loop, tubular fluid is highly concentrated. This is the descending limb's contribution to countercurrent multiplication.
Incorrect. The thin descending limb does not actively transport Cl−; transport is restricted to passive water loss.
Incorrect. ROMK is found in the thick ascending limb and collecting duct, not the thin descending limb.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old researcher demonstrates that the thin ascending limb of Henle is permeable to NaCl but impermeable to water — the inverse of the descending limb. Which of the following best explains the passive efflux of NaCl in the thin ascending limb?
choices: Active NKCC2 cotransport in the thin ascending limb
ADH-stimulated water reabsorption that secondarily concentrates NaCl
Passive Na+ and Cl− diffusion down concentration gradients
Aldosterone-driven Na+ reabsorption
Bicarbonate-driven anion exchange
explanations: Incorrect. NKCC2 is expressed in the THICK ascending limb; the THIN ascending limb has no significant active NaCl transport.
Incorrect. The thin ascending limb is impermeable to water; ADH does not concentrate the tubular fluid here.

Correct. The thin ascending limb is water-impermeable but NaCl-permeable. Tubular fluid arriving at the bottom of the loop is highly concentrated (because water was removed in the descending limb). As fluid ascends through the increasingly less hypertonic interstitium, NaCl diffuses passively down its concentration gradient out of the tubular fluid into the medullary interstitium. This passive contribution complements the active NaCl transport of the TAL above. Note: in the inner medulla, urea (recycled from the inner medullary collecting duct under ADH) is the dominant osmolyte rather than NaCl.
Incorrect. Aldosterone acts on collecting duct principal cells, not the thin ascending limb.
Incorrect. Bicarbonate handling is a feature of the PCT (and intercalated cells), not the thin ascending limb.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old researcher studies the thick ascending limb of Henle. The diagram below summarizes the principal apical and basolateral transporters of the TAL. The lumen-positive transepithelial voltage generated in this segment drives paracellular reabsorption of which of the following pairs of cations?
questions.diagram:
Thick ascending limb (TAL) ion transport
Apical: NKCC2 (Na+, K+, 2Cl− into cell) — site of loop diuretic action
Apical: ROMK recycles K+ back to the lumen → lumen-positive voltage
Basolateral: Na+/K+-ATPase, ClC-Kb (Cl− out)
Water IMPERMEABLE → 'diluting segment' of the nephron
Lumen-positive voltage drives paracellular cation reabsorption via claudin-16/19
choices: Na+ and K+
Mg2+ and Ca2+
H+ and HCO3−
PO4³⁻ and SO4²⁻
Cl− and HCO3−
explanations: Incorrect. Na+ and K+ are reabsorbed transcellularly via NKCC2, not paracellularly.

Correct. NKCC2 brings Na+, K+, and 2Cl− into the TAL cell from the lumen; K+ then recycles back into the lumen via apical ROMK. This recycling generates a LUMEN-POSITIVE transepithelial voltage. The positive lumen drives paracellular reabsorption of cations — specifically Mg2+ and Ca2+ — through tight-junction claudin-16/19 channels. Mutations in CLDN16 or CLDN19 cause familial hypomagnesemia with hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis.
Incorrect. H+ and HCO3− are not the principal paracellular movers in the TAL.
Incorrect. PO4³⁻ and SO4²⁻ are not paracellularly transported via this voltage gradient.
Incorrect. Cl− is reabsorbed transcellularly via NKCC2 + basolateral ClC-Kb; HCO3− is not the relevant ion at this segment.

questions.stem: A 6-year-old boy is evaluated for poor growth, polyuria, and salt craving. He has been small for his age throughout life and is in the third percentile for height. Laboratory studies are shown.
choices: Loss-of-function mutation in NCC (DCT)
Gain-of-function mutation in ENaC (CD)
Loss-of-function mutation in AQP2 (CD)
11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase deficiency (apparent mineralocorticoid excess)
Loss-of-function mutation in NKCC2 (TAL) — Bartter syndrome
explanations: Incorrect. Loss-of-function NCC mutations cause Gitelman syndrome, which differs in showing HYPOcalciuria (not hypercalciuria) and is typically diagnosed in adolescence/adulthood rather than early childhood.
Incorrect. Gain-of-function ENaC produces Liddle syndrome, characterized by HYPERTENSION, low renin, low aldosterone — opposite of this profile.
Incorrect. AQP2 mutations produce nephrogenic diabetes insipidus with polyuria and hypernatremia, not the hypokalemic alkalosis seen here.
Incorrect. AME features hypertension, suppressed renin/aldosterone, with the metabolic alkalosis and hypokalemia mimicking aldo excess. The high renin/aldo and low BP rule it out here.

Correct. Bartter syndrome is caused by loss-of-function mutations in TAL transporters (NKCC2, ROMK, ClC-Kb, or barttin). Loss of NKCC2 abolishes both transcellular NaCl reabsorption and the lumen-positive voltage required for paracellular Mg2+ and Ca2+ reabsorption — producing hypomagnesemia and HYPERcalciuria. Volume contraction activates RAAS (high renin, high aldosterone), and increased distal Na+ delivery drives K+ secretion (hypokalemia) and H+ secretion (metabolic alkalosis). BP is typically NORMAL or LOW, distinguishing it from Liddle and AME.

questions.stem: A 28-year-old researcher demonstrates that the lumen-positive transepithelial voltage in the thick ascending limb drives paracellular Mg2+ and Ca2+ reabsorption. Through which tight-junction claudin proteins is this paracellular cation flux mediated?
choices: Claudin-2 (favoring monovalent cations)
Claudin-4 (favoring small anions)
Claudin-7 (favoring water)
Claudin-16 and claudin-19 (paracellular Mg2+ and Ca2+ pore in the TAL)
Claudin-1 (favoring large molecules)
explanations: Incorrect. Claudin-2 is enriched in the PCT, where it forms cation-permeable 'leaky' tight junctions for monovalent cations.
Incorrect. Claudin-4 favors anions and is not the relevant TAL pore for Mg2+/Ca2+.
Incorrect. Claudin-7 has tissue-specific roles but is not the principal Mg2+/Ca2+ paracellular pore in the TAL.

Correct. The TAL expresses claudin-16 and claudin-19 in tight junctions, which together form the paracellular pore for Mg2+ and Ca2+ that the lumen-positive voltage drives. Mutations in CLDN16 or CLDN19 cause familial hypomagnesemia with hypercalciuria and nephrocalcinosis (FHHNC), often presenting in childhood with renal failure, hypomagnesemia, and stone disease.
Incorrect. Claudin-1 is widely expressed in barrier-type epithelia (e.g., epidermis) but is not the relevant TAL paracellular cation pore.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with chronic heart failure is started on furosemide 40 mg daily. Compared with no diuretic, which row in the table best describes the expected effect of loop diuretic therapy on his urinary excretion of these ions?
choices: A
B
C
D
E
explanations: Correct. Loop diuretics block NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb. This reduces transcellular NaCl reabsorption (↑ urinary Na+) and abolishes the lumen-positive voltage that drives paracellular Mg2+ and Ca2+ reabsorption (↑ urinary Ca2+, ↑ urinary Mg2+). Increased distal Na+ delivery drives aldosterone-mediated K+ secretion (↑ urinary K+). Net pattern: all three are increased. Loop diuretics are useful in hypercalcemia for this reason and contrast with thiazides, which lower urinary Ca2+.
Incorrect. ↑Na+, ↑K+, ↓Ca2+ describes thiazide diuretic action (NCC block in DCT lowers urinary Ca2+ via secondary mechanisms — useful in stone prevention).
Incorrect. Loop diuretics raise (not lower) urinary K+ via increased distal Na+ delivery to the collecting duct.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics increase urinary Na+ excretion; this is their natriuretic mechanism.
Incorrect. Loop diuretics produce significant changes in all three; they are not 'unchanged.'

questions.stem: A 28-year-old researcher is studying the distal convoluted tubule. The principal apical sodium transporter of the early DCT is NCC, the thiazide-sensitive Na+-Cl− cotransporter. Which of the following best characterizes NCC?
choices: Active ATP-dependent pump in the apical membrane
Electroneutral apical Na+/Cl− cotransporter inhibited by thiazides
Apical NKCC2-like transporter requiring K+
ENaC-mediated electrogenic Na+ uptake
Aquaporin water channel
explanations: Incorrect. NCC is not directly ATP-dependent; it is a secondary active cotransporter exploiting the Na+ gradient.

Correct. NCC is an electroneutral apical Na+-Cl− cotransporter expressed in the early distal convoluted tubule. It reabsorbs ~5% of filtered Na+, secondary-actively powered by the Na+ gradient maintained by basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase. NCC is inhibited by thiazide diuretics (e.g., hydrochlorothiazide) and is loss-of-function in Gitelman syndrome (autosomal recessive, presents in adolescence/adulthood with hypokalemic alkalosis, hypomagnesemia, and HYPOcalciuria — distinguishing it from Bartter syndrome).
Incorrect. NCC does not require K+; it transports only Na+ and Cl−.
Incorrect. ENaC is the apical Na+ channel of collecting duct PRINCIPAL CELLS, not the DCT.
Incorrect. Aquaporins are water channels; NCC transports Na+ and Cl−.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old woman with hypertension and recent calcium oxalate stones is started on hydrochlorothiazide. Which of the following best describes the principal mechanism of action of thiazide diuretics?
choices: Inhibition of NKCC2 in the thick ascending limb
Inhibition of ENaC in collecting duct principal cells
Inhibition of carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
Antagonism of the mineralocorticoid receptor in collecting duct principal cells
Inhibition of NCC in the early distal convoluted tubule
explanations: Incorrect. NKCC2 inhibition is the loop diuretic mechanism, not thiazide.
Incorrect. ENaC inhibition is the mechanism of amiloride and triamterene.
Incorrect. Carbonic anhydrase inhibition is the mechanism of acetazolamide.
Incorrect. MR antagonism is the mechanism of spironolactone and eplerenone.

Correct. Thiazides inhibit NCC in the early DCT, reducing apical Na+/Cl− cotransport. The natriuresis produces volume contraction, which paradoxically enhances proximal Na+ AND Ca2+ reabsorption (passive 'tag-along'). Reduced intracellular Na+ in DCT cells also enhances basolateral Na+/Ca2+ exchanger (NCX1) activity and apical TRPV5-mediated Ca2+ uptake. The net effect is hypocalciuria — clinically useful for prevention of recurrent calcium stones and contrasting with the hypercalciuria of loop diuretics.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with primary hyperaldosteronism has elevated aldosterone secretion from an adrenal adenoma. Aldosterone binds the cytosolic mineralocorticoid receptor in collecting duct principal cells. Which set of transporters is upregulated by mineralocorticoid receptor activation in these cells?
choices: NKCC2, ROMK, basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase
NCC, ENaC, basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase
Apical ENaC, apical ROMK, and basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase
SGLT2, NHE3
Carbonic anhydrase II and IV
explanations: Incorrect. NKCC2 is in the TAL and is not regulated by aldosterone.
Incorrect. NCC is in the DCT; while there is some aldosterone-induced regulation of NCC (via WNK kinases), the principal aldosterone targets are in the principal cell.

Correct. Aldosterone bound to the mineralocorticoid receptor enters the nucleus and increases transcription of genes encoding apical ENaC subunits (faster Na+ entry into the cell), apical ROMK (faster K+ exit into the lumen), and basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase subunits (more vigorous basolateral pumping). Together these increase Na+ reabsorption and K+ secretion in the principal cell, with downstream H+ secretion at adjacent α-intercalated cells (the lumen-negative voltage created by Na+ reabsorption favors H+ secretion).
Incorrect. SGLT2 and NHE3 are PCT transporters and are not aldosterone targets in the collecting duct.
Incorrect. Carbonic anhydrase isoforms are PCT enzymes for HCO3− reclamation.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old man with severe hypertension since age 22 has a strong family history (his father was on dialysis by age 50). His current laboratory studies are shown.
choices: Conn syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism)
Bartter syndrome
Gitelman syndrome
Apparent mineralocorticoid excess from licorice ingestion (11β-HSD2 deficiency)
Liddle syndrome — gain-of-function ENaC mutation in collecting duct
explanations: Incorrect. Conn syndrome would feature ELEVATED aldosterone with suppressed renin; this patient has BOTH suppressed.
Incorrect. Bartter syndrome features LOW or normal blood pressure and HIGH renin/aldosterone, opposite of this profile.
Incorrect. Gitelman also features low/normal BP and elevated renin/aldosterone, plus hypomagnesemia and hypocalciuria.

Incorrect. AME (e.g., from licorice/glycyrrhizic acid inhibiting 11β-HSD2) shares the phenotype but is acquired and reversible with steroid treatment or licorice withdrawal; it would be unusual in a young man with strong family history of premature ESRD.

Correct. Liddle syndrome is an autosomal-dominant gain-of-function mutation in the β or γ subunit of ENaC (deletion of a PY motif that normally targets ENaC for endocytic degradation by the ubiquitin ligase Nedd4). The result is constitutively activated apical Na+ channels in collecting duct principal cells, with mineralocorticoid-independent Na+ reabsorption, K+ secretion, and H+ secretion. Phenotype: severe hypertension at a young age, hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis, suppressed renin and aldosterone (contrast with Conn). Treatment is amiloride or triamterene (direct ENaC blockers); spironolactone/eplerenone do NOT work because the lesion is downstream of the mineralocorticoid receptor.

questions.stem: A male newborn is admitted at age 5 days for severe failure to thrive, dehydration, and persistent salt-wasting. Laboratory studies show profound hyponatremia (Na+ 122), hyperkalemia (K+ 7.2), and metabolic acidosis. Plasma aldosterone and plasma renin activity are markedly ELEVATED. Volume status is depleted. Which of the following best characterizes this disorder?
choices: Liddle syndrome — gain-of-function ENaC mutation
Conn syndrome — primary hyperaldosteronism
Bartter syndrome — NKCC2 loss-of-function
Pseudohypoaldosteronism type 1 — mineralocorticoid resistance
Type 1 (distal) renal tubular acidosis
explanations: Incorrect. Liddle syndrome has hypertension, hypokalemia, suppressed renin/aldosterone — opposite profile.
Incorrect. Conn syndrome features hypertension and hypokalemia from aldosterone excess.
Incorrect. Bartter features hypokalemia, alkalosis, and normal-low BP — opposite of the hyperkalemic acidosis here.

Correct. PHA1 is a syndrome of mineralocorticoid resistance. The autosomal recessive form (severe, multisystem) is caused by loss-of-function mutations in ENaC subunits, producing salt wasting from kidney, sweat glands, and intestine; the autosomal dominant form (milder, kidney-limited) is caused by mutations in the mineralocorticoid receptor. The kidney cannot respond to aldosterone, so Na+ is not reabsorbed and K+ is not secreted in the collecting duct — yielding hyponatremia, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, and volume depletion. Aldosterone and renin levels are HIGH but ineffective at the kidney. Treatment is salt supplementation and potassium control.
Incorrect. Type 1 RTA features HYPOkalemia and inability to acidify urine, not the hyperkalemic acidosis here.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old man with primary hyperaldosteronism (Conn syndrome) has chronically elevated plasma aldosterone. Compared with a healthy individual at baseline, which row best describes the effect of aldosterone on the collecting duct?
choices: A
B
C
D
E
explanations: Correct. Aldosterone bound to the mineralocorticoid receptor in collecting duct principal cells increases transcription of ENaC, ROMK, and basolateral Na+/K+-ATPase. Apical ENaC activity rises, drawing Na+ into the cell and creating a lumen-negative voltage; this drives K+ secretion via ROMK and H+ secretion at adjacent α-intercalated cells. Net effect: increased urinary K+ and H+, with metabolic alkalosis and hypokalemia clinically characteristic of mineralocorticoid excess.
Incorrect. ↓ENaC, ↓K+ secretion, ↓H+ secretion describes the OPPOSITE situation — aldosterone deficiency (Addison disease) or PHA1.
Incorrect. Aldosterone enhances H+ secretion (metabolic alkalosis), not suppresses it.
Incorrect. Aldosterone increases (not decreases) ENaC activity.
Incorrect. Mineralocorticoid excess produces clear changes in all three parameters — they are not unchanged.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with HFrEF is started on spironolactone for both diuretic and mortality benefit. Within two weeks, urinary potassium excretion has fallen and serum potassium has risen modestly. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of action of spironolactone?
choices: Direct ENaC inhibition (similar to amiloride and triamterene)
Direct ROMK inhibition reducing K+ secretion
Competitive antagonism of the mineralocorticoid receptor on principal cells
Inhibition of 11β-hydroxysteroid dehydrogenase type 2
V2 vasopressin receptor antagonism
explanations: Incorrect. Direct ENaC inhibition is the mechanism of amiloride and triamterene — distinct from spironolactone's MR antagonism.
Incorrect. Spironolactone does not directly inhibit ROMK; it works upstream through MR antagonism.

Correct. Spironolactone is a competitive antagonist of the cytosolic mineralocorticoid receptor in collecting duct principal cells. By preventing aldosterone from inducing transcription of ENaC, ROMK, and Na+/K+-ATPase, it reduces Na+ reabsorption (natriuresis), reduces K+ secretion (potassium-sparing), and reduces downstream H+ secretion at α-intercalated cells. Spironolactone also has antiandrogenic effects (gynecomastia, decreased libido) due to nonselective binding to androgen and progesterone receptors; eplerenone is a more selective MR antagonist with fewer such effects.
Incorrect. 11β-HSD2 inhibition is the mechanism by which licorice (glycyrrhizic acid) produces apparent mineralocorticoid excess; this is not spironolactone's action.
Incorrect. V2 receptor antagonism is the mechanism of tolvaptan, used in SIADH and selected ADPKD patients.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old man with severe vomiting from gastroenteritis develops metabolic alkalosis with serum HCO3− 34 mEq/L. The kidney's α-intercalated cells of the collecting duct contribute to acid-base homeostasis. In this setting of metabolic ALKALOSIS, β-intercalated cells are upregulated. Which of the following best describes the mechanism of the α-intercalated cell (the cell type relevant in metabolic ACIDOSIS)?
choices: Apical Na+/H+ exchanger and basolateral Na+/HCO3− cotransporter
Apical H+-ATPase with basolateral Cl−/HCO3− exchanger (band 3)
Apical Cl−/HCO3− exchanger (pendrin) secreting HCO3− with basolateral H+-ATPase (this is β-intercalated)
Apical K+ recycling via ROMK driving paracellular acid secretion
Apical Na+/HCO3− cotransport delivering bicarbonate to the lumen
explanations: Incorrect. NHE3 + basolateral Na+/HCO3− cotransport is the PCT mechanism for bicarbonate reclamation; α-intercalated cells use a different machinery.

Correct. α-Intercalated cells secrete H+ into the lumen via apical H+-ATPase (and a smaller contribution from H+/K+-ATPase, which is upregulated in hypokalemic alkalosis). On the basolateral side, the Cl−/HCO3− exchanger (band 3 / AE1) extrudes HCO3− into blood. Cytoplasmic carbonic anhydrase II generates the H+ and HCO3− substrate from CO2 + H2O. In metabolic acidosis, α-intercalated cells are upregulated, generating new bicarbonate to titrate the acid load.
Incorrect. This describes β-intercalated cells, with reversed transporter polarity. β-Intercalated cells are upregulated in metabolic alkalosis.
Incorrect. K+ recycling via ROMK is not the principal mechanism of α-intercalated cell H+ secretion.
Incorrect. α-Intercalated cells do not deliver bicarbonate to the lumen; they secrete H+ into the lumen.

questions.stem: A 32-year-old woman with active vomiting from cyclic vomiting syndrome develops metabolic alkalosis (HCO3− 34 mEq/L). The β-intercalated cell of the collecting duct is upregulated to help excrete the excess bicarbonate. Which of the following best describes the transporter polarity of the β-intercalated cell?
choices: Apical H+-ATPase and basolateral Cl−/HCO3− exchanger (this is the α-intercalated cell)
Apical Cl−/HCO3− exchanger (pendrin) secreting HCO3− into the lumen, with basolateral H+-ATPase returning H+ to the blood
Apical Na+/Cl− cotransporter (NCC)
Apical Na+/H+ exchanger (NHE3)
Apical AQP2 water channel
explanations: Incorrect. This is the α-intercalated cell pattern, upregulated in acidosis (not alkalosis).

Correct. β-Intercalated cells have an APICAL Cl−/HCO3− exchanger (pendrin) that secretes bicarbonate into the lumen in exchange for chloride entry, and a BASOLATERAL H+-ATPase that exports H+ to blood. The polarity is the mirror image of the α-intercalated cell. β-Intercalated cells are upregulated in metabolic alkalosis, where they contribute to bicarbonate excretion. Pendrin loss-of-function mutations cause Pendred syndrome (sensorineural deafness with goiter), while pendrin upregulation in metabolic alkalosis is part of the renal compensatory response.
Incorrect. NCC is in the DCT, not the collecting duct intercalated cells.
Incorrect. NHE3 is the apical Na+/H+ exchanger of the PCT.
Incorrect. AQP2 is the apical water channel of principal cells, not intercalated cells.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man maximally stimulated to concentrate his urine (e.g., during severe water deprivation) has concentrated medullary interstitium that depends on urea recycling. Which of the following best describes the renal handling of urea under maximal ADH stimulation?
choices: Urea is freely filtered, neither reabsorbed nor secreted
Urea is actively secreted by the proximal tubule
Urea is reabsorbed via UT-A1/A3 in the inner medullary collecting duct
Urea is excluded from the kidney by the glomerular filtration barrier
Urea is metabolized by tubular cells to ammonia
explanations: Incorrect. Urea is freely filtered, but it is variably reabsorbed and secreted along the nephron — and ADH specifically upregulates urea reabsorption in the inner medullary collecting duct.
Incorrect. Urea movement is largely passive; the proximal tubule reabsorbs urea passively (more so when flow is slow), and it is not actively secreted.

Correct. Under maximal ADH stimulation, the urea transporters UT-A1 and UT-A3 in the apical and basolateral membranes of the inner medullary collecting duct are upregulated. This permits urea movement out of the tubule into the inner medullary interstitium, where urea contributes substantially (~half) of the inner medullary osmolality of ~1200 mOsm/kg. This 'urea recycling' allows the kidney to excrete urea efficiently while still concentrating urine maximally — without urea recycling, the obligate urea load would osmotically prevent concentration of the urine.
Incorrect. Urea is small (~60 Da) and freely filtered.
Incorrect. Urea is not appreciably metabolized by tubular cells; ammoniagenesis is from glutamine, a separate pathway.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old researcher is studying how the loops of Henle generate and maintain the medullary osmotic gradient required for urinary concentration. Which of the following best describes the principle of countercurrent multiplication?
choices: Vasa recta countercurrent EXCHANGE alone establishes the gradient
Active urea pumping in the inner medulla concentrates the interstitium
ADH-mediated water removal at the loop of Henle directly removes water from the descending limb
Aldosterone-driven Na+ retention concentrates the medulla
Active NaCl pumping by the TAL with osmotic equilibration in the descending limb
explanations: Incorrect. Vasa recta perform countercurrent EXCHANGE that PRESERVES the gradient, but they do not establish it; the loops of Henle establish the gradient.
Incorrect. Urea recycling contributes to the gradient (especially in the inner medulla), but it is passive (driven by UT-A1/A3 under ADH), not active pumping.
Incorrect. ADH acts at the COLLECTING DUCT principal cell, not the loop of Henle. The loop creates the gradient that ADH-driven water reabsorption in the collecting duct then exploits.
Incorrect. Aldosterone acts on the collecting duct principal cell and is not the mechanism by which the medullary osmotic gradient is generated.

Correct. Countercurrent multiplication is the cyclic process by which the parallel descending and ascending limbs of Henle, working together, generate the medullary osmotic gradient. The water-impermeable thick ascending limb actively transports NaCl from tubular fluid to interstitium via NKCC2, raising interstitial osmolality. The water-permeable descending limb then equilibrates osmotically by passively losing water through AQP1, concentrating tubular fluid. The stepwise transfer is amplified by the parallel arrangement, creating a stable gradient up to ~1200 mOsm/kg at the renal papilla — the osmotic 'engine' that allows the collecting duct, under ADH, to concentrate urine.

questions.stem: A 25-year-old researcher studies the vasa recta. Vasa recta blood flow is intentionally low and the descending and ascending vasa recta lie in parallel hairpin loops alongside the loops of Henle. Which of the following best describes the principal function of this arrangement?
choices: Active pumping of solutes into the medullary interstitium
Direct production of urine in the medulla
Maximizing oxygen delivery to the inner medulla
Passive countercurrent exchange that preserves the medullary osmotic gradient
Filtering plasma a second time in the medulla
explanations: Incorrect. Vasa recta are passive blood vessels; they do not pump solutes.
Incorrect. Urine is produced in the tubular system (PCT, loop of Henle, DCT, collecting duct), not by vasa recta blood vessels.

Incorrect. Medullary blood flow is intentionally LOW to preserve the osmotic gradient; this means the inner medulla operates at the lowest tissue PO2 in the kidney — the opposite of 'maximizing oxygen delivery.'

Correct. Vasa recta are fenestrated capillaries that descend and ascend in close apposition with the loops of Henle. As blood descends into the medulla, NaCl and urea diffuse INTO it from the interstitium and water diffuses OUT, equilibrating the blood with the surrounding hyperosmolar interstitium. As blood ascends, the reverse occurs — solutes diffuse OUT and water diffuses IN. This countercurrent EXCHANGE means that solutes and water are passively shuttled around the hairpin loop without being carried away in net transport, so the medullary osmotic gradient (created by the loops of Henle) is not 'washed out.' Slow blood flow through vasa recta is essential to this preservation.
Incorrect. Filtration occurs only at the glomerulus; vasa recta do not filter plasma.
